title: Johnson and Johnson Pulls Tylenol
text:
In late September 1982 seven people in the Chicago area died after taking Extra-Strength Tylenol capsules. Someone had laced capsules with cyanide and put the bottles back on store shelves. Tylenol was then the best-selling painkiller in the United States, and the killer was never caught.

The company, led by chairman James Burke, did not know at first whether the poisoning had happened in its factories. It warned the public not to use Tylenol capsules, stopped advertising, worked openly with the police, the FBI and the press, and then recalled every bottle of Tylenol capsules in the country, around 31 million bottles, at a cost of about 100 million dollars. Burke appeared on television to explain what the company was doing. The poisoning turned out to have happened after the products left the factory.

Within weeks Johnson and Johnson reintroduced Tylenol in new triple-sealed, tamper-resistant packaging, and offered to swap capsules for tablets. Tylenol's market share collapsed after the deaths, but within about a year it had largely recovered. The response became a standard case in business schools.
lesson: In a crisis, protect the people who depend on you first and tell them the truth. Short-term cost spent on trust usually comes back.
source: Contemporary press coverage; Harvard Business School case studies on the Tylenol crisis
